title: From Indonesia, living in Delhi
title_target: मैं इंडोनेशिया से हूँ — maiⁿ inDoneshiyaa se huuⁿ
goal: Say where you're from, where you live, and what you do — and meet an idea that turns English habits around: Hindi "prepositions" stand AFTER the noun.
bekal: name cities and countries with में and से
say what you do, in the feminine form too
use the six most common postpositions

dialogs.title: संवाद — A cup of tea with Rahul's mother
dialogs.intro: Ani is invited for tea next door. Rahul's mother asks the things every Indian will ask you in the first ten minutes. Watch where words like से, में, and पर go: all of them come after the noun, not before.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: I — Indonesia — from — am, Jakarta — from.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: ji — yes. here — from — seven — hours.

lines.speaker: माँ जी:
lines.id: And now you live in Delhi?
lines.literal: and — now — you — Delhi — in — living(fem.) — are?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Yes, I live right here. I work at a school.
lines.literal: ji, I — right-here — living(fem.) — am. I — one — school — in — work — doing(fem.) — am.

lines.speaker: माँ जी:
lines.id: I see! Are you a teacher?

lines.speaker: माँ जी:
lines.id: Very good. Is everyone well at home?
lines.literal: very — good. home — at — all — fine — are?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Yes, everyone's fine. My parents are in Jakarta.
lines.literal: ji, all — fine — are. my — mother-father — Jakarta — in — are.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Every day, on the phone. I miss them a lot.
lines.literal: every — day, phone — on. they — to-me — very — memory — coming — are.

notes: **The big idea of this unit: what English puts BEFORE the noun, Hindi puts AFTER it.** "In Delhi" becomes **दिल्ली में** (Delhi–in). "From Indonesia" becomes **इंडोनेशिया से** (Indonesia–from). "On the table" becomes **मेज़ पर** (table–on). That's why they're called **postpositions** (*परसर्ग*), not prepositions. ⚠️ It feels backwards for a week or two, then stops feeling like anything. A trick: read from the back. मेज़ पर = "table … on".

**कहाँ से हैं? — notice where the question word goes.** English moves it to the front ("Where are you from?"); Hindi keeps it just before the verb, near the end. आप **कहाँ से** हैं? आप **कहाँ** रहती हैं? आप **क्या** करती हैं? Putting it first sounds like machine translation.

**में, पर, and से — three postpositions that cover almost every A1 sentence.** **में** = inside something with space (कमरे में, दिल्ली में, बैग में). **पर** = on a surface or at a point (मेज़ पर, फ़ोन पर, घर पर). **से** = from, with, or using (जकार्ता से, चम्मच से, उनसे). ⚠️ "At home" is **घर पर**, not घर में — it means "at that address", not "inside the building". घर में means literally inside the house.

**Job titles have feminine forms, and you must use your own.** अध्यापक (male teacher) → अध्यापि**का**; छात्र (student) → छात्रा; लेखक (writer) → लेखिका. But many modern jobs don't change at all: **डॉक्टर, इंजीनियर, मैनेजर, पायलट** are used as they are for anyone. ⚠️ And most important: **there's no "a"**. *मैं अध्यापिका हूँ* = "I'm (a) teacher". Adding एक there isn't wrong, but it sounds like you're counting.

**एक means "one" and sometimes works like "a"**, but far less often than English *a/an*. *मैं एक स्कूल में काम करती हूँ* uses एक because it means "some school, never mind which". If both speakers already know the school, एक disappears. When in doubt, leave it out — Hindi is much stingier with "a" than English.

**तो in the third line doesn't mean "so".** In the middle of a sentence like this it just adds emphasis, like English "really" or "you know": *वह तो बहुत दूर है* = "That's really far, you know". Little words like ही, भी, and तो are what make Hindi sound alive; you'll pick them up from the dialogues, not from a list.

**बेटी and बेटा ("daughter", "son") are used for younger people, even by people you've just met**, and they're a sign of warmth, not cheek. Taxi drivers, shopkeepers, and the aunties next door will call you बेटा or बेटी. ⚠️ Don't answer with the same word; reply with **आंटी जी** (auntie), **अंकल जी** (uncle), or **भैया** (big brother) and **दीदी** (big sister) for people your age. Family terms are used for strangers all day long in India, and using them instantly makes you sound like an insider.

grammars.title: Six postpositions that cover almost everything
body: Learn these six now. Everything else is a combination of them.
after: ⚠️ **Pronouns change shape as soon as a postposition follows them** — मैं becomes मुझ, वह becomes उस, वे becomes उन. Think *I → me*, *he → him*. This is your first taste of the **oblique form**, covered fully in unit 7. For now, learn the pairs in the table; there are few of them and they're used every day.

grammars.title: Countries, languages, and jobs
after: ⚠️ Indians call their own country **भारत** (*bhaa-rat*) in Hindi and **इंडिया** in English. Both are everyday words, but भारत sounds warmer when you say it in a Hindi sentence.

blocks.text: You'll hear these three questions many times a day. Each answer needs just one pattern; only the details change.

head: Question
Pronunciation
Sample answer
rows: मैं एक स्कूल में काम करता हूँ।
आपके घर में कौन कौन है?
aap-ke ghar meⁿ kaun kaun hai

blocks.title: Questions that may surprise you
items: **आपकी शादी हुई है?** — "Are you married?" Asked within the first ten minutes, by anyone, with no hidden meaning. Answer **जी हाँ** or **जी नहीं, अभी नहीं** (not yet).
**आपकी उम्र क्या है?** — "How old are you?" Just as casual. Your age decides what people call you, so it's genuinely useful information, not small talk.
**आप कितना कमाते हैं?** — "How much do you earn?" This can come up too. If you'd rather not say, **बस ठीक-ठाक** ("just okay") with a smile is enough and isn't considered rude.
⚠️ None of these questions is rude. In many Indian families, asking them is actually a sign that you're being accepted as one of them, not an outsider.

blocks.text: One sentence you'll need often: **मुझे घर की याद आती है** (*mu-jhe ghar kii yaad aa-tii hai*) — "I miss home". Literally "to me memory of home comes", and that backwards order is no accident; units 8 and 16 show that many Hindi feelings are built this way — the feeling comes to you, rather than you feeling it.
